job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Jamal Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I finished electrical engineering at Manchester in June, and since October I've been a junior protection engineer at a firm that builds substations. Most days I'm checking relay settings in a spreadsheet, drafting test sheets, and twice a week I'm out at a substation in a van with an older engineer called Dennis. I rent a room in Salford with two guys, and my dad, who's an electrician, rings me every night to ask what I learned.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment when a protection scheme trips exactly as the sheet says it should. What wears me out is the paperwork, honestly, because every test needs a signed report and the templates are ancient. I'm also paying off about 18,000 of loan, and I have two months of rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the world stays predictable. I use an AI chat tool now and then to tidy my test reports, and it saves me twenty minutes. If that's all it ever does, brilliant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel relieved. The grid needs engineers whatever happens, and there's a shortage of people who can sign off protection work. My pay is typical for a grad, but it's going up if I pass my first-year review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working towards my professional registration and keep using the tool for reports. I'd also join the union branch at work, because I think it's good to be in one from the start. I'd put 150 a month on the loan and keep building to four months of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My work and money feel secure enough, though the loan is always there in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why join the union if nothing is changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you join before you need it. My dad was in the electricians' union for thirty years, and the one time the firm tried to cut overtime pay, they had a rep who knew what to say. I want that in place for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the loan interest went up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my overtime straight to the loan and stop going out on Fridays. It's a squeeze, not a disaster.

say: I'd say good, a **predictable** world suits me and the grid still needs engineers.
I'd tell colleagues to join the **union** branch before they need it.
think: Privately I feel **relieved**, since few people can sign off protection work.
My only background worry is the **loan**, about 18,000.
do: Pass my first-year review and keep building towards **professional registration**.
Put **150 a month** on the loan and save up to four months of rent.
feel: **Calm**, with the loan sitting quietly at the back of my mind.
S0.quote: My dad was in the electricians' union for thirty years, and the one time the firm tried to cut overtime pay, they had a rep who knew what to say.
fieldNote: He is secure in a job with a **shortage of skills**, and the mood follows his money and work, not his tone.
His union habit comes from his father, an electrician, and it shapes how he plans every scenario.
Say and think agree; the loan is his only background pressure.

steps.text: Pass the first-year review and log hours towards registration
Join the union branch at work this month
Put 150 a month on the loan and build four months of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, so we need rules and training now. Our test reports and relay setting spreadsheets are exactly the kind of work software takes over. I'd tell the union branch to ask the firm for a written plan on how juniors get trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit nervous. The junior's job of checking and writing up tests is the part AI does well, so the firm might hire fewer juniors and give more work to the ones left. But somebody still has to climb a ladder and check a relay, and the robots arrive later in the hands-on side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI properly, not just for reports: draft test sheets, check calculations, then verify by hand. I'd volunteer for the field work with Dennis, because that's the part software can't do soon. I'd also take a short course on grid automation that the firm offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but alive. It's the first time I think my degree needs a second skill on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be your second skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Commissioning, I think, meaning switching on new equipment on site and being the person who finds why it didn't work. It's practical and you have to be there. I'd also want to be able to read what the software did, so I can explain it to the customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guy who does the drawings in the next room, Aiden. He's been there fifteen years and does nothing but update CAD sheets. If anyone's chair is empty first, it's his.

say: I'd say the change is real, so we need **rules and training** now.
I'd ask the union branch to get a written **plan for training juniors**.
think: Checking and writing up tests is what AI does well, so the firm may hire **fewer juniors**.
Hands-on field work arrives later, so I want to be **on site**.
do: Use AI to draft test sheets, then **verify by hand** before signing.
Volunteer for **field work** with Dennis and take the firm's grid automation course.
feel: **Uneasy but alive**; my degree now needs a second skill on top.
S1.quote: Somebody still has to climb a ladder and check a relay, and the robots arrive later in the hands-on side.
fieldNote: He answers with a **plan**, not a complaint, which fits his steady, open-to-proven-change style.
He names a colleague, Aiden, as the likely first casualty, a sign he thinks about **others** too.
Say and think are close; the nerves show only in private.

steps.text: Draft test sheets with the AI tool and verify each one by hand
Volunteer for site commissioning visits with Dennis
Ask the union branch for a written plan for training juniors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast and we need government and unions to act now. I'd go to a rally if the union called one, and I'd write to my MP about income support and retraining funded by the companies that profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. By 2028 I'll be 24 with a loan and a job that exists to check things an AI can check better. Robots on site take three more years, so I'd have maybe 2031 as the real deadline for field work. I'm not sure I'm good enough to be one of the few people kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every spare pound and cut my rent by moving back in with my parents, which my dad already offered. I'd go all in on commissioning and field work, so that I'm the person on site. I'd also ask the union what the plan for members is, and organise colleagues to ask the firm the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quick pulse. But not frozen, because I think there's still something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Dad, you've been telling me it's a safe trade for ten years, so tell me how safe it is now. He'd say wires don't run themselves, and I'd want to believe him. Then he'd ring the union and ask who's in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does moving back home feel like failing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But my parents' house has a spare room and no rent, and if two years is all we've got, I'd rather have the money than my pride.

say: I'd say two years is too fast and **government and unions** must act now.
I'd write to my MP about income support paid for by the firms that **profit**.
think: By 2028 I'll be 24 with a loan and a job that **checks things** AI checks better.
I'm not sure I'm good enough to be **one of the few** kept.
do: Move back with my parents to save **rent** and clear the loan faster.
Go all in on **commissioning and field work** so I'm the person on site.
feel: **Anxious**, with a quick pulse, but not frozen because there is still something to do.
S2.quote: If two years is all we've got, I'd rather have the money than my pride.
fieldNote: The fear is about his **own worth**, not only the economy, and it surprised me.
He turns the fear into steps quickly: parents' spare room, **field skills**, union questions.
His father's calm trust in wires is a counterweight he half believes.

steps.text: Move back into the parents' spare room and stop paying rent
Put the rent saved straight onto the student loan
Ask the union what plan exists for members and organise colleagues
Write to my MP about funded retraining and income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a sensible plan, but only if somebody makes one. I'd press the union to bargain for a training fund and for a rule that the firm shares what it saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's the one I find hardest to read. By 2031 I'll be 27 and a senior-ish engineer, so I might be the person who survives. But if the thinking part is automated in 2031 and the hands-on part by 2034, the fastest-growing job will be the one who supervises machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to be that person. I'd finish registration in the next three years, push towards commissioning and then project work, and keep using AI every week so I know what it gets wrong. I'd buy a flat share with a mate if I got the chance, rather than throw rent at a landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. A bit of excitement, a bit of dread, like the night before a first day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you knew it was exactly 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend 2027 and 2028 learning everything I could on the job and be cheap and useful to my boss. By 2030 I'd have a savings target, a year's rent in the bank, because I don't trust anyone to look after me once it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that the same plan as with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not quite. With ten, I can afford a master's or a proper career turn; with five I'd rather stay in the job and train inside it.

say: I'd say five years is enough for a **sensible plan** if somebody makes one.
I'd push the union for a **training fund** and a share of savings.
think: By 2031 I'll be 27 and might be among those who **survive**.
The fastest-growing job will be **supervising machines**, and I want that job.
do: Finish **registration** within three years, then move towards commissioning and project work.
Save **a year of rent** by 2030 and use AI weekly to learn its mistakes.
feel: **Mixed**: a bit of excitement and a bit of dread, like the night before a first day.
S3.quote: With ten, I can afford a master's or a proper career turn; with five I'd rather stay in the job and train inside it.
fieldNote: He compares the windows carefully and says what **each length** changes, which is rare.
He plans around **staying and training inside** the firm, not leaving it.
He doesn't trust anyone to look after him afterwards, so he saves first.

steps.text: Finish professional registration within three years
Use the AI tool every week and keep a list of its errors
Save a full year of rent by 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it well. I'd say every apprenticeship and graduate scheme should be rewritten now so that it still makes sense in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm fairly calm. Ten years takes me to 32, with registration and maybe a team to lead. I'd have time to try a master's in power systems and AI, and the grid's still being built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, finish the registration, then do a part-time master's in about three years. I'd stay in the union and maybe become the rep. And I'd start putting 300 a month into a pension, not just the loan, because ten years is long enough for it to matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit hopeful. It's the one where I get to be a person who helped shape it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hopeful about what exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful that the grid needs people to build it for decades, and that unions get a say in the deal. If the gains are shared, I'm all for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the gains aren't shared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be angry and I'd be in the union meeting every week, shouting about it.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if apprenticeships and graduate schemes are rewritten now.
I'd back **unions** having a real say in how AI gains are shared.
think: Ten years gets me to 32 with registration and perhaps a **team to lead**.
The grid is still being built, so I feel fairly **calm**.
do: Finish registration, then start a part-time **master's in power systems** in about three years.
Pay **300 a month** into a pension as well as the loan, and stand for union rep.
feel: **Calm** and a bit hopeful; I'd get to help shape how it goes.
S4.quote: Hopeful that the grid needs people to build it for decades, and that unions get a say in the deal.
fieldNote: This is the only scenario where his hope outweighs his fear, and he ties it to **shared gains**.
He sees himself as a future **union rep**, which shows how much identity he draws from his father.
Conditional optimism: if gains aren't shared, he'll be angry and active.

steps.text: Finish registration then start a part-time master's in power systems
Stand as the union rep at work
Pay 300 a month into a pension as well as the loan
Keep working on substation protection jobs with Dennis

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years, because there's no time to put a plan in place and my own loan runs for decades. What would help is a training fund, a union bargaining seat on how AI is used at work, and some form of income support if jobs vanish. I'd also want firms to pay for retraining before they let people go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not a pessimist. I think there'll be plenty of work building the grid, but I'd like us to decide together who benefits.

headlineQuote: I think there'll be plenty of work building the grid, but I'd like us to decide together who benefits.
portrait: Jamal is a 22-year-old **electrical engineer** in his first job at a substation contractor near Manchester, with about 18,000 of student loan.
He is steady and open to change once it's proven, and he **uses AI** for reports now and then.
His father, an electrician and union man, shapes his instinct to **organise** and to ask who benefits.
He is calm when the grid still needs people and **anxious** only when two years leaves no time for a plan.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries him most, because there'd be no time to pay off the loan or build a plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **training fund**, a union seat in decisions about AI at work, and income support if jobs disappear.
